response_text: Always selecting the task with the numerically highest priority is attractive in theory but disastrous in practice when combined with cooperative yielding. A single highest-priority task can monopolise the CPU simply by failing to call yield(), starving every lower-priority task indefinitely. Even if the system is modified to pre-empt on a timer, strict “run the highest” scheduling introduces fairness and latency problems: lower-priority housekeeping or I/O tasks may wait unbounded amounts of time, potentially violating real-time deadlines. The policy also creates opportunities for priority inversion, where a low-priority task holds a shared resource needed by a high-priority task, blocking the latter unless extra priority-inheritance mechanisms are added. For these reasons, real systems either combine priority with round-robin time slices inside each level or employ ageing algorithms that gradually boost the priority of long-waiting tasks.\n
